WHMIS Overview — What It Is and Why It Matters

Who this lesson is for

You. Every person who works at Southbrook Cabinetry — shop floor, finishing room, warehouse, office, delivery driver, summer student — takes this lesson on hire and once a year after that. It does not matter whether you ever pour a litre of lacquer thinner; if you set foot in the shop, you are covered by WHMIS and you need to know what it is.

This is a base awareness lesson. It does not make you certified to run the spray booth, to operate the forklift, or to handle the acid catalysts used with some conversion varnishes. Those tasks have their own hands-on training and sign-off. WHMIS is the foundation everyone shares.

Where this lives on the site

This course is delivered through Southbrook's online learning portal:

southbrookcabinetry.space → eLearning → WHMIS Base Training

The supporting paperwork lives in the shop, not online:

Floor Office → SDS Binder (physical binder — exact shelf location: TBD, trainer to fill in)

Shared drive → Safety → SDS (electronic backup of every binder sheet)

You sign an attendance record after the in-person walkthrough of this course; the record is kept for at least three years per Ontario OHS expectations.

What you'll see in the shop

WHMIS shows up in three places on the floor. Once you know what they look like, you stop missing them.

  • Labels on every container of a hazardous product. A 4 L can of lacquer thinner from the supplier has a printed label with red-diamond pictograms, a signal word ("Danger" or "Warning"), and a list of precautions. When you decant some of that thinner into a smaller squirt bottle for cleanup, that bottle gets a workplace label — see lesson 16.3.
  • Safety Data Sheets (SDS) — one paper sheet per product, filed in the SDS binder. Each is a 16-section document the supplier writes. Lesson 16.4 walks you through it.
  • Training — this course, plus job-specific training when your role involves handling a particular product (spray booth, finishing, glue line). Training is the third pillar; without it, the labels and SDSs are just paper.

Recognition + response

What WHMIS is. WHMIS stands for Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System. It is the Canada-wide system that tells you what hazardous chemicals are in your workplace and how to use them safely. It has been law since 1988. The current version — WHMIS 2015 — aligns Canada with the Globally Harmonized System (GHS), which is the international standard the United Nations adopted so a chemical labelled in Germany or Japan looks the same to a Canadian worker reading the container.

The three pillars. WHMIS works because three things happen together:

  1. Labels on every container.
  2. Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) available to every worker.
  3. Education and training so workers can read both.

Remove any one of the three and the system fails. A perfect label on a sealed drum is useless if you cannot read it. A binder full of SDSs is useless if no one ever opens it.

The legal frame. WHMIS is split across federal and provincial law:

  • Federal — the Hazardous Products Act and the Hazardous Products Regulations set the rules suppliers and importers must follow when they sell a hazardous product into Canada. That is why the label on a can of lacquer thinner shipped from Ohio looks the way it does — the importer had to bring it into compliance.
  • Provincial / territorial — each province's Occupational Health and Safety Act sets the rules employers and workers must follow once the product is in the workplace. Southbrook operates in Ontario, so Ontario's OHS Act and Reg. 860 (WHMIS) govern what we do here.

If you ever move to a shop in another province, the federal piece is identical and the provincial piece will look very similar — the three pillars do not change.

Employer responsibilities. Southbrook (your employer) must:

  • Make sure every hazardous product in the shop has a current supplier label or a workplace label.
  • Keep a current SDS for every hazardous product, accessible to workers.
  • Provide WHMIS education (this course) and job-specific training.
  • Review the training at least annually and whenever a new hazard is introduced.

Your responsibilities. As an employee you must:

  • Complete WHMIS training and the annual refresher.
  • Read labels and follow the precautions before you use a product.
  • Use the personal protective equipment (PPE) specified for the job.
  • Report damaged labels, missing SDSs, leaks, spills, or unsafe conditions to your supervisor — without waiting.
  • Ask if you do not know. There is never a wrong time to ask about a chemical.

Bilingual rule. In Canada, supplier labels and SDSs must be available in both English and French. If you find a container with only one language, that is a compliance gap — tell your supervisor.

Common mistakes + how to recover

"It's just a small amount, I don't need to read the label."

The amount in the container has nothing to do with the hazard of the product. A 250 mL squirt bottle of lacquer thinner is just as flammable as a 4 L can. Read the label.

"I've used this product for years, I know what it does."

Formulations change. The chemistry of a finish product can be updated by the supplier between batches. The label and the SDS are the source of truth, not your memory. Skim them when a new batch shows up.

"There's no SDS in the binder for this product."

Stop using the product. Tell your supervisor. Southbrook is legally required to have one and the supplier is legally required to provide it. This is not a small problem — it is the system failing.

"My English is weak and the label is hard for me to read."

The label has to be in English and French. Pictograms are designed to be understood without words. Ask your supervisor for the French label or for someone to walk through it with you. WHMIS is built so that no worker ever has to guess.

Quiz (5 questions, applied)

1. A coworker hands you a clear plastic squeeze bottle of liquid and says "use this to wipe down the panels before staining." There is no label on the bottle. What do you do?

Do not use it. An unlabelled container is a WHMIS violation. Ask the coworker what is in it and have them apply a proper workplace label (product name, safe-handling precautions, reference to the SDS) before you go near it. If they cannot tell you what is in it, treat it as unknown and tell your supervisor.

2. Which of the following is not one of the three pillars of WHMIS? (a) Labels, (b) Safety Data Sheets, (c) Education and training, (d) First-aid kits.

(d) First-aid kits. First aid is required under provincial OHS law but it is not a WHMIS pillar. The three WHMIS pillars are labels, SDSs, and education/training.

3. A new can of contact cement arrives from the supplier. The label is printed only in English — there is no French. Is this a problem?

Yes. WHMIS 2015 requires supplier labels to be in both English and French. Tell your supervisor; Southbrook may need to apply a bilingual workplace label or contact the supplier for a corrected label.

4. Whose job is it to make sure the SDS binder is up to date?

The employer's — Southbrook's. The supplier provides the SDSs at point of sale; Southbrook maintains the binder and keeps it accessible to workers. Your job is to use it and to report when an SDS is missing.

5. A summer student starts on Monday and is sent to help in the finishing room. They have not taken WHMIS training yet. What does Southbrook owe them before they handle any product?

WHMIS education before they work with or near hazardous products. Ontario OHS does not allow "we'll train you later." The student takes this base lesson first, then the job-specific finishing-room training, then they can go near the product.

What this lesson does NOT cover

  • The 9 GHS pictograms in detail → lesson 16.2.
  • Supplier vs workplace label specifics → lesson 16.3.
  • How to read an SDS → lesson 16.4.
  • The specific hazardous products you'll meet at Southbrook → lesson 16.5.
  • Your right to refuse unsafe work and the emergency-response steps → lesson 16.6.
  • Hands-on certification for the spray booth, forklift, or any specific machine — those have separate training programs.
The 9 WHMIS Pictograms — What They Mean
article
Every Southbrook employee.

The 9 WHMIS Pictograms — What They Mean

Who this lesson is for

Every person at Southbrook. Pictograms are the fastest way to identify a hazard — they are designed so you can recognise the risk across the shop floor without reading the label up close. You should be able to look at a container at three metres and know whether it is flammable, toxic, corrosive, or none of the above.

Where this lives on the site

Pictograms appear on every supplier label and on every SDS (Section 2). Reference posters are on the wall:

Finishing Room → wall by the SDS binder (WHMIS pictogram poster)

Shop entrance → safety board (WHMIS pictogram poster)

If a poster is missing or damaged, tell your supervisor — Southbrook is required to keep the visual reference posted.

What you'll see in the shop

Each pictogram is a black symbol inside a red diamond on a white background, points up and down. A black-and-white diamond is not a current WHMIS 2015 pictogram — it is either an obsolete WHMIS 1988 symbol (suppliers were required to transition by Dec 2018) or a non-WHMIS warning. Flag it.

Recognition + response

1. Flame

Visual. A flame shape inside the red diamond. Means. Flammable gases, liquids, solids; pyrophoric materials; self-heating substances; self-reactive compounds. At Southbrook. Lacquer thinner, mineral spirits, nitrocellulose lacquers, denatured alcohol, acetone, contact cement, most aerosols, propane cylinders. Response. No open flames, no sparks, no smoking. Use only in ventilated areas. Bond and ground when transferring. Know the nearest fire extinguisher (Class B for flammable liquids).

2. Flame Over Circle

Visual. A flame on top of a circle (the circle = oxygen). Means. Oxidizer. The product itself may not burn, but it feeds a fire so it burns hotter and faster. At Southbrook. Less common — some bleaches, peroxide wood-bleach products, warehoused pool/spa chemicals. Response. Keep oxidizers physically away from flammables — not in the same cabinet or shelf. Fires involving oxidizers are hotter and harder to put out.

3. Gas Cylinder

Visual. A pressurized gas cylinder. Means. Gases under pressure — compressed, liquefied, refrigerated, or dissolved. The hazard is the pressure itself plus whatever the gas does. At Southbrook. Propane cylinders for the forklift. Some aerosols. Response. Cylinders stored upright, chained, valve caps on when not in use. Never drop, never expose to heat. Forklift-propane changes require certification — get trained first.

4. Corrosion

Visual. Two test tubes pouring liquid onto a hand and a metal bar, both being eaten away. Means. Destroys metals and burns skin and eyes on contact. At Southbrook. Acid catalysts used with conversion varnishes. Some metal-prep chemicals. Strong cleaners. Response. Chemical-resistant gloves (not leather), face shield, apron. Know where the eye-wash station is before you open the container. Splash to the eye is a 15-minute flush, immediately.

5. Exploding Bomb

Visual. A black explosion with chunks flying outward. Means. Explosive. Self-reactive substances (Type A/B) and organic peroxides (Type A/B) that can detonate or undergo violent runaway reactions. At Southbrook. Very rare. Some organic-peroxide finish catalysts carry this in concentration. If you ever see this on a container, stop and call your supervisor — it should not be a routine item. Response. Treat as the most hazardous thing in the room. No heat, shock, or friction.

6. Skull and Crossbones

Visual. A human skull with two crossed bones. Means. Acute toxicity — a single short exposure (swallowing, skin contact, or vapour inhalation) can kill or seriously injure. At Southbrook. Rare but real. High-concentration acid catalysts, some stripping chemicals, methanol if used as a solvent. Response. Full PPE per the SDS — gloves, respirator (correct cartridge), eye protection, sometimes face shield. Use only in the spray booth or other properly ventilated area. Wash hands before eating, drinking, smoking. If exposed: SDS Section 4 (first aid) + eye-wash or shower immediately.

7. Health Hazard

Visual. A human torso silhouette with a starburst on the chest, suggesting internal-organ damage. Means. Longer-term or chronic effects. Carcinogens (cancer), mutagens (genetic damage), reproductive toxins, respiratory sensitizers (cause asthma after repeated exposure), aspiration hazards, organ toxicity from repeated exposure. At Southbrook. Solvent-based contact cement. Some lacquers and stains with isocyanates or formaldehyde-releasing resins. Methylene chloride strippers (legacy stock). Petroleum distillates in older mineral spirits. Response. Engineering controls first — spray-booth ventilation, local exhaust. PPE second — respirator with the SDS-specified cartridge, gloves. The hazard is cumulative — every exposure matters.

8. Exclamation Mark

Visual. A single black exclamation mark. Means. Lower-severity hazards. Skin and eye irritation, skin sensitization (allergic dermatitis from repeated contact), acute toxicity that is harmful but not fatal at typical exposures, respiratory irritation. At Southbrook. Most water-based finishes. PVA / yellow wood glue. Many cleaning solvents. Some edge-banding hot-melt adhesives. Wood dust is treated under this category in some SDSs. Response. Skin and eye protection, good ventilation. This is the "won't put you in hospital today, but will mess you up over a career" warning. Wear gloves even when "it's just glue."

9. Biohazardous Infectious Materials

Visual. The trefoil biohazard symbol (three interlocking arcs). Means. Biological agents — bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, or the toxins they produce. This is the one pictogram Canada kept from WHMIS 1988 that is not in international GHS. At Southbrook. Effectively never. If you see it here, stop and call your supervisor. Response. Do not handle without specific training.

Note on the "environment" pictogram. GHS includes an optional Environment pictogram (dead fish + dead tree) for aquatic hazards. Canada did not adopt this for workplace WHMIS — you will not see it on Canadian WHMIS 2015 supplier labels. It may appear on SDS Section 12 or transport documents, but not in the red diamond on the container.

Common mistakes + how to recover

"The container has two pictograms — which one matters more?" Both do. A can of lacquer thinner often carries Flame, Exclamation Mark, and Health Hazard together. Follow the precautions for all.

"It's an old can from 2012 and the symbols look different." That can carries WHMIS 1988 symbols (circles, not diamonds). Suppliers were required to transition by Dec 2018. Flag it — outdated symbols may also mean outdated hazard info.

"The label is damaged and I can only see one pictogram." Apply a workplace label or replace the supplier label. Do not guess at missing information. See lesson 16.3.

"I confuse Skull and Crossbones with Health Hazard." The split is timing. Skull and Crossbones = a single exposure can hurt you now. Health Hazard = repeated exposure damages you over time. A product can carry both.

Quiz (5 questions, applied)

1. You walk past a 1 L bottle in the finishing room and see two red diamonds: Flame and Health Hazard. Without reading any words, what does that tell you?

The product is flammable (no sparks, ventilate) and causes long-term health damage on repeated exposure (use the respirator specified on the SDS — never skip PPE because "it's only a little"). Both apply at the same time.

2. A can of contact cement shows Flame, Exclamation Mark, and Health Hazard. Skull and Crossbones is not present. Does that mean it is safe to drink?

No. Skull and Crossbones marks acute toxicity — short, severe exposures. Many things are not in the acute category and are still toxic to swallow. Check SDS Sections 4 (first aid) and 11 (toxicology). Never drink anything in the shop.

3. You see the Exploding Bomb pictogram on a small bottle on the finishing-room shelf. What do you do?

Stop. Call your supervisor. The Exploding Bomb is rare in a cabinet shop and should not be a routine item. Verify with the SDS what is in the bottle and whether it should be there at all.

4. A coworker tells you "this can has the Corrosion pictogram, but it's only Category 2, so the gloves we use for staining are fine." How do you respond?

Check the SDS, not the assumption. The Corrosion pictogram means the product burns skin and damages metals — solvent-rated gloves are not necessarily corrosive-rated. SDS Section 8 specifies the correct glove material (often nitrile, neoprene, sometimes butyl) and the eye-wash must be in reach before you open the container.

5. You see a pictogram with the trefoil biohazard symbol on a container in the warehouse. Is this a normal Southbrook product?

No. The Biohazardous Infectious Materials pictogram is for biological agents. It has no routine use in cabinet manufacturing. Stop and call your supervisor — something is mis-shelved or mis-shipped.

What this lesson does NOT cover

  • Supplier vs workplace labels → lesson 16.3.
  • How to read an SDS for the exact glove, respirator, and first aid → lesson 16.4.
  • The specific Southbrook products that carry each pictogram, with PPE detail → lesson 16.5.
  • Emergency exposure or spill response → lesson 16.6.
  • Hands-on PPE fit-testing — your job-specific training covers that.
Labels — Supplier and Workplace
article
Every Southbrook employee.

Labels — Supplier and Workplace

Who this lesson is for

Every Southbrook employee. You read labels every time you pick up a container of finish, glue, solvent, or cleaner. You apply labels whenever you pour a product into a smaller container — for the spray gun, for a wipe bottle, for a touch-up jar. Getting the label right is the easiest part of WHMIS to do wrong, and the easiest to fix.

Where this lives on the site

Workplace-label blanks (pre-printed peel-and-stick sheets) live next to the relevant decanting stations:

Finishing room → solvent decant station → workplace-label dispenser (exact location: TBD, trainer to fill in)

Glue area → adhesive decant station → workplace-label dispenser

If a dispenser is empty, ask your supervisor for a fresh roll before you decant.

What you'll see in the shop

There are two kinds of WHMIS labels at Southbrook:

  1. Supplier labels — printed by the manufacturer or importer, on the container the product arrived in. Big, glossy, bilingual.
  2. Workplace labels — printed or written on at Southbrook, applied when we pour the product into a different container. Small, plain, may be hand-written.

You also see transport / hazard placards on shipping pallets and delivery trucks. Those are governed by Transport Canada (TDG), not WHMIS, and are out of scope for this lesson — but if you see one on a delivery that does not match the supplier label, flag it.

Recognition + response

Supplier label — the six required elements

Every WHMIS 2015 supplier label, by law, contains six things. If any one of them is missing, the label is incomplete and the product should not be used until corrected.

  1. Product identifier — the name of the product. Brand, chemical, common, or trade name. It must match what is in the SDS Section 1. Example: "M.L. Campbell Magnamax Pre-Cat Lacquer."
  2. Initial supplier identifier — name, address, and telephone of the Canadian manufacturer or importer. This is who is legally accountable for the product on the Canadian market.
  3. Pictogram(s) — the red-diamond hazard symbols (lesson 16.2). Zero, one, or several depending on the hazard profile.
  4. Signal word — exactly one of "Danger" or "Warning". - "Danger" is for the more severe hazard categories. - "Warning" is for the less severe ones. - If the product has no signal word, it is not classified as hazardous under WHMIS.
  5. Hazard statement(s) — standardized phrases describing the nature of the hazard. Example: "Highly flammable liquid and vapour. May cause respiratory irritation." These phrases are not freeform — they come from a fixed list set by the regulations.
  6. Precautionary statement(s) — what to do to use the product safely. Example: "Keep away from heat / sparks / open flames / hot surfaces. No smoking. Wear protective gloves / eye protection."

A typical Southbrook supplier label also carries the product code / batch number and fill date — useful but not legally required.

Bilingual rule

Supplier labels in Canada must appear in both English and French. Either on one bilingual label or on two labels (English on one side, French on the other) attached to the same container. A unilingual supplier label is not compliant — tell your supervisor; Southbrook will need to apply a bilingual workplace label or get a corrected label from the supplier.

Workplace label — what we apply at Southbrook

When you pour a product out of the supplier container into a smaller container — squirt bottle, jar, cup, secondary tank — that smaller container needs a workplace label unless one of two exceptions applies (covered below).

A workplace label needs three elements:

  1. Product identifier — the same name that appears on the SDS, so anyone reading the workplace label can look up the SDS.
  2. Safe handling precautions — basic precautions (may include pictograms). Does not have to be the full list from the supplier label, but should cover the headline hazard.
  3. Reference to the SDS — wording that points the reader to the SDS for full information (e.g. "See SDS for full handling instructions.").

Workplace labels do not need to be bilingual unless your workforce needs both languages. Southbrook applies bilingual workplace labels by default — it is good practice and removes ambiguity.

Two exceptions where you do not need a workplace label:

  • Decant for immediate use. You pour the product, you use it in the same shift, the container stays under your control the whole time, and the leftover is properly disposed of or returned at end of shift. The spray-booth pot is the classic case.
  • The original container is undisturbed. Obvious — supplier label still attached, still legible, still intact.

If the product is sitting overnight in a smaller container, even one you plan to finish tomorrow, it needs a workplace label.

"Danger" vs "Warning" — a closer look

These are not interchangeable. The supplier picked one based on the hazard category and you should react to it:

  • Danger = high-severity category. Lacquer thinner gets "Danger" for flammability. An acid catalyst gets "Danger" for corrosion or acute toxicity. Treat the precautions as non-negotiable.
  • Warning = lower-severity category. PVA glue typically gets "Warning" for skin/eye irritation. Still real, still requires PPE, but the failure mode is irritation rather than acute injury.

Damaged, missing, or illegible labels

If you pick up a container and the supplier label is torn, faded, washed off, painted over, or written in a language you cannot read — stop.

The procedure is:

  1. Do not use the product.
  2. Set the container aside in a safe location (not on the spray-booth bench, not next to an ignition source).
  3. Tell your supervisor.
  4. Your supervisor confirms what is in the container — by checking the stock record, the SDS binder, or the supplier — and either applies a new workplace label or quarantines the container for disposal.

Do not try to identify the contents by smell, colour, or "what we usually keep here." The whole point of the labelling system is that nobody guesses.

Common mistakes + how to recover

"I'm decanting lacquer into a small jar for touch-up — but I'm using it right now, so I don't need a label."

Correct only if the jar stays with you and gets disposed of (or poured back) at the end of your shift. If you leave it on the bench overnight, the next person to pick it up has no way to know what is in it. Label it.

"The supplier label got soaked in lacquer thinner and the words are gone. I know it's lacquer thinner — I just opened it."

It does not matter that you know. The next person to walk up to the container does not. Apply a workplace label or replace the supplier label.

"I cut the supplier label off and threw it away because it was peeling — I'll put a workplace label on later."

You created an unlabelled hazardous container. The few minutes between "now" and "later" are when something goes wrong. Label it before you set it down.

"This label only has English on it — but I can read English so it's fine."

It is not fine. The next worker who picks it up may not read English. Bilingual is a legal requirement for the supplier label, not a politeness.

"It's a workplace label, so I'll just write the product name and skip the safe-handling precautions."

A workplace label needs three things, not one. If the safe-handling precautions section is missing, the label does not meet WHMIS requirements. The pre-printed peel-and-stick blanks have all three fields — fill them all in.

Quiz (5 questions, applied)

1. You decant 500 mL of lacquer thinner from the 4 L supplier can into a clean glass jar so you can take it to the assembly bench for cleanup. You will use roughly half of it today, then put the jar in your cabinet at the end of shift to use again tomorrow. Does the jar need a workplace label?

Yes. Because the jar will sit unattended (in your cabinet, after shift), the "immediate use" exception does not apply. Apply a workplace label with product name, safe-handling precautions, and a reference to the SDS before you leave for the day. Bilingual is Southbrook's standard practice.

2. A new shipment of contact cement arrives. The supplier label shows pictograms, a signal word "Danger," hazard statements, and precautionary statements — but no manufacturer address or phone number. Is the label compliant?

No. The initial supplier identifier (name, address, telephone of the Canadian manufacturer or importer) is one of the six required elements. Tell your supervisor; Southbrook needs to follow up with the supplier for a corrected label.

3. A coworker hands you a bottle with a workplace label that says only "Glue." The bottle is sitting on the assembly bench. What is missing, and what do you do?

The workplace label needs the product name as it appears on the SDS, safe-handling precautions, and a reference to the SDS. "Glue" is not a product name (PVA, contact cement, hot melt, and epoxy are all "glue"). Have the coworker re-label with the actual product or replace the label before you use it.

4. Two pictograms appear on a container — Flame and Health Hazard — with the signal word Warning. Are you safe to skip the respirator because the signal word is not "Danger"?

No. The signal word reflects the highest severity category among the hazards classified. "Warning" still means real hazard. The Health Hazard pictogram drives respirator use — check SDS Section 8 for the required cartridge regardless of whether the signal word is "Danger" or "Warning."

5. You find a 250 mL squeeze bottle in the spray booth with a faded, illegible label. The liquid inside smells like solvent. What is the right next step?

Do not use it. Set it aside in a safe location. Tell your supervisor. Identifying by smell is not allowed under WHMIS — your supervisor verifies the contents from the stock record or the SDS binder and either applies a new workplace label or disposes of the container.

What this lesson does NOT cover

  • The 9 WHMIS pictograms in detail → lesson 16.2.
  • How to read and use an SDS → lesson 16.4.
  • The specific hazardous products you'll meet at Southbrook → lesson 16.5.
  • Transport Canada (TDG) shipping placards — different system, see Southbrook's Receiving training.
  • What to do when there is a spill, an exposure, or a fire → lesson 16.6.
Safety Data Sheets — Reading the SDS
article
Every Southbrook employee.

Safety Data Sheets — Reading the SDS

Who this lesson is for

Every Southbrook employee. The SDS is the document you open before you use a new product, when something goes wrong, and after an exposure to give to the medical responder. It is your primary reference. It is also the document most workers have never actually read — this lesson fixes that.

Where this lives on the site

Southbrook keeps SDSs in two places, both kept in sync:

Floor Office → SDS Binder (physical binder, alphabetised by product name — exact shelf location: TBD, trainer to fill in)

Shared drive → Safety → SDS (electronic backup, searchable by product name)

The physical binder is the version you grab in an emergency — it does not need power or a login. The electronic version is for quick lookup from your computer when you are planning work.

If an SDS is missing for a product on the shelf, that is a compliance gap. Tell your supervisor — they will pull it from the supplier and file it.

What you'll see in the shop

Every SDS in Canada follows the same structure: 16 sections in a fixed order, set by WHMIS 2015 / GHS. The format does not vary by supplier — Sherwin-Williams, M.L. Campbell, Titebond, and 3M all publish the same 16 sections in the same order. Once you know the order, you can find anything in any SDS in under 30 seconds.

The SDS is bilingual — English and French. Both languages must be provided, either as one bilingual document or as two simultaneous unilingual documents.

Recognition + response

The 16 sections — what is in each

The first nine sections are the ones a shop-floor worker uses. The last seven (10–16) are technical and regulatory — useful for the supervisor, the safety officer, and emergency responders.

Sections 1–9 — work-floor essentials:

  1. Identification. Product name, supplier name + address + phone, emergency telephone number, recommended use. This is the section you read to confirm you have the SDS for the right product.
  2. Hazard identification. Classification, pictograms, signal word ("Danger" / "Warning"), hazard statements, precautionary statements. This is the "what's the worst thing this can do to me" summary.
  3. Composition / information on ingredients. Chemical names, CAS numbers, concentration ranges of the hazardous ingredients. Useful if you ever have to tell a doctor what is in the product.
  4. First-aid measures. What to do for inhalation, skin contact, eye contact, and ingestion. Read this before you open the container so you know the response if something happens. Also tells you when to call a doctor and what symptoms to watch for.
  5. Fire-fighting measures. Suitable extinguishing media (water? foam? CO2? dry chemical?), unsuitable extinguishing media, special fire-fighting hazards. Critical if you ever face a fire involving the product.
  6. Accidental release measures. What to do for a small spill vs a large spill. Containment. Cleanup. PPE for the cleanup.
  7. Handling and storage. Safe handling practices. Storage conditions — temperature, ventilation, incompatibilities (what can't go on the same shelf).
  8. Exposure controls / personal protection. Exposure limits (e.g. 8-hour TWA), engineering controls (spray booth, local exhaust), and the exact PPE you need — glove material, eye protection, respirator cartridge type, body protection.
  9. Physical and chemical properties. Appearance, odour, flash point, viscosity, vapour pressure. Useful for confirming you have the right product, and the flash point tells you how easily it ignites.

Sections 10–16 — technical / regulatory:

  1. Stability and reactivity. Conditions to avoid, incompatible materials, hazardous decomposition products.
  2. Toxicological information. Routes of exposure, symptoms, acute and chronic effects, LD50 data.
  3. Ecological information. Environmental impact. (Disclosure optional in some cases.)
  4. Disposal considerations. How to dispose of the product and contaminated packaging.
  5. Transport information. UN number, shipping name, transport hazard class.
  6. Regulatory information. Applicable safety, health, and environmental regulations.
  7. Other information. Date of preparation or last revision. An SDS older than 3 years should be flagged — the supplier is required to update it on a 3-year cycle (or sooner if significant new info comes to light).

The five sections you actually use as a worker

If you remember only five, remember these:

  • Section 2 — hazards. What is the worst this can do.
  • Section 4 — first aid. What to do if it lands on you, in you, or in your eye.
  • Section 6 — accidental release. What to do if it spills.
  • Section 7 — handling and storage. How to use it without it going wrong.
  • Section 8 — PPE. What to wear so it does not go wrong in the first place.

If you have 60 seconds before starting a new product, read these five.

How to look up an SDS at Southbrook

  1. Find the product name on the supplier label (Section 1 of the SDS will match it). The product name, not the brand — "Magnamax Pre-Cat Lacquer," not "Campbell."
  2. Open the Floor Office SDS Binder to that letter. Alphabetised by product name.
  3. Pull the sheet. Read the five core sections (2, 4, 6, 7, 8).
  4. Return the sheet to the binder when done — do not take it back to the shop floor and lose it.

If you cannot find the SDS, do not open the container. Use the electronic copy on the shared drive instead, or ask the supervisor to pull it from the supplier.

When to read an SDS

  • First time you use a product.
  • When a new shipment arrives and the date of revision (Section 16) is newer than the one in your binder.
  • Annually, as part of this refresher.
  • Immediately if there is a spill, an exposure, a fire, or a near miss involving the product.
  • Before any non-routine handling (transferring large quantities, mixing two products, disposing).

Common mistakes + how to recover

"I've used this lacquer for 5 years, I don't need to look at the SDS."

Suppliers reformulate. A change of resin chemistry can change the respirator cartridge type, the glove material, or the flash point. Skim Section 16 of the new shipment's SDS — if the revision date is newer than your binder copy, replace the binder copy and re-read Sections 2 and 8 before use.

"The product spilled, I'll look up the cleanup procedure after I mop it up."

No. Read Section 6 first — some products require neutralization, some must not be mopped (creates more vapour), some require a respirator for cleanup. Cleaning up wrong can be worse than the spill.

"The doctor asked what I was exposed to — I just told him 'lacquer thinner.'"

That is a start, but the SDS is what the doctor actually needs. Section 3 (composition) and Section 11 (toxicology) tell the doctor what to watch for and how to treat. Bring or send the SDS with the person to the hospital.

"There's no SDS for this product."

Then the product cannot be used at Southbrook. The employer is legally required to have one; the supplier is legally required to provide one. Tell your supervisor — this is a fix-today problem.

"The SDS is dated 2018 — five years old."

WHMIS 2015 requires SDSs to be updated within 3 months when significant new hazard information becomes available, and reviewed regularly. A 5-year-old SDS may not reflect the current formulation or current regulatory classification. Tell your supervisor to request the latest revision from the supplier.

Quiz (5 questions, applied)

1. You're about to spray a new conversion varnish you've never used before. You have 5 minutes before the booth is free. Which sections of the SDS do you read in that 5 minutes?

Sections 2 (hazards — pictograms, signal word, hazard statements), 8 (PPE — which respirator cartridge, glove material, eye/face protection), and 4 (first aid — what to do if you splash it on yourself). Section 6 (spill) and Section 7 (handling) are next if you have time. Save 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 for your supervisor.

2. A coworker has a chemical splash to the eye. Which SDS section tells you what to do?

Section 4 — first-aid measures. It will tell you the eye-wash duration (typically 15 minutes minimum), whether to remove contact lenses, and when to call a doctor. Get to the eye-wash station first, read the section while the eye is being flushed, do not delay the flush.

3. You spill 4 L of lacquer thinner on the finishing-room floor. You reach for the mop. What should you have done first?

Read Section 6 — accidental release measures. Lacquer thinner is flammable; mopping it spreads the vapour and the vapour can ignite from any spark. Section 6 will tell you to ventilate, eliminate ignition sources, and use absorbent (not water and not a mop) to contain it. Many spills also require a respirator for cleanup — Section 8 of the same SDS specifies which cartridge.

4. The SDS for a product is dated July 2018. Today is June 2026. What do you do?

Tell your supervisor and request the latest revision from the supplier. Suppliers are required to keep SDSs current. An 8-year-old SDS may not reflect the current formulation, current hazard classification, or current first-aid practice. Until the new revision arrives, the 2018 sheet is the reference you have — use it, but do not assume it is up to date.

5. Whose responsibility is it to make sure the SDS binder has a current SDS for every hazardous product on the Southbrook shop floor?

The employer — Southbrook. The supplier is required to provide SDSs at point of sale; the employer is required to maintain them and keep them accessible to workers. Your job as a worker is to use the binder, report missing or outdated sheets to your supervisor, and follow the instructions inside.

  • Emergency response — spills, fires, exposures, evacuation → lesson 16.6.

Hazardous Materials in YOUR Cabinet Shop

Who this lesson is for

Every Southbrook employee, with extra attention from anyone on the shop floor. By the end of this lesson you can name every significant chemical and physical hazard in your normal day, recognise the pictograms it carries, and know what to do if it lands on you, catches fire, or spills. This is about our specific products, not a generic list.

Where this lives on the site

Floor Office → SDS Binder (exact shelf location: TBD, trainer to fill in)

Shared drive → Safety → SDS (electronic backup)

Finishing room → respirator cabinet + glove dispenser

Glue area → safety-glasses + nitrile-glove dispenser

What you'll see in the shop

Below are the nine hazards grouped by where they show up in workflow. For each: what it is, hazard type + pictograms, PPE, and what to do if exposed or spilled.

Recognition + response

1. Wood dust

What it is. Particulate from sawing, routing, sanding, edge-banding trim-back. Includes hardwood dust (oak, maple, walnut, cherry, cedar) and engineered-product dust (MDF, particleboard, melamine).

Hazard + pictograms. Combustible dust — fine dust suspended in air ignites readily; cyclones and ducts are explosion-rated for a reason. Respiratory carcinogen — oak, walnut, cedar, beech are classified as nasal/sinus carcinogens with long-term exposure. MDF dust contains formaldehyde resin binders (respiratory irritant). Some species cause skin sensitization. Pictograms on packaged MDF: Health Hazard, Exclamation Mark.

PPE. Safety glasses, N95 minimum for sanding (higher-rated respirator for prolonged work or when dust collection is down), long sleeves, hearing protection at sanders. Wash hands before eating.

If exposed. Eye: flush. Skin reaction: wash, note the species, tell supervisor. Heavy inhalation: fresh air, doctor if breathing affected.

If spilled / accumulated. Never use compressed air (re-suspends dust, explosion risk). HEPA vacuum or sweep with dust-suppressing compound. Keep collection bin from overflowing.

2. Solvent-based finishes (lacquers, stains, conversion varnishes)

What it is. Nitrocellulose and pre-cat lacquers, post-cat (acid-cured) conversion varnishes, oil-based stains, solvent dyes.

Hazard + pictograms. Flame (flash points often below 25 °C), Exclamation Mark (irritation, sensitization), Health Hazard (toluene, xylene, glycol ethers — chronic liver/kidney/CNS effects).

PPE. Half-face or full-face respirator with organic-vapour cartridges (cartridge type is on SDS Section 8). Nitrile or solvent-rated chemical gloves — leather is not solvent-rated. Safety glasses, face shield for high-volume spray.

If exposed. Skin: wash with soap and water, do not use solvent. Eye: 15-minute eye-wash, medical attention. Inhalation: fresh air, supervisor notified. Ingestion: do not induce vomiting, call Poison Control, bring SDS.

If spilled. Small (under ~1 L): eliminate ignition sources, ventilate, absorb with clay/vermiculite, dispose in approved metal waste container. Large: evacuate, alert supervisor. Never mop, never use water, no electrical switches in vapour area.

3. Acid catalysts (for conversion varnishes)

What it is. Catalysts (often para-toluene sulfonic acid) mixed into post-cat varnishes to cure them. Sold in small bottles.

Hazard + pictograms. Corrosion (skin/eye burns), sometimes Skull and Crossbones (acute toxicity), Health Hazard (respiratory sensitization).

PPE. Butyl or neoprene gloves (not standard nitrile — check SDS), face shield, chemical apron, respirator with cartridge specified on the SDS. Eye-wash within 10 seconds reach before opening the bottle.

If exposed. Skin: 15-minute flush, remove contaminated clothing, seek medical attention. Eye: 15-minute eye-wash, immediate medical attention. Ingestion: do not induce vomiting, call Poison Control, bring SDS.

If spilled. Small: neutralize per SDS Section 6 (often sodium bicarbonate slurry), absorb, dispose as hazardous waste. Large: evacuate, alert supervisor, do not approach without full PPE.

4. Contact cement / edge-banding adhesives

What it is. Solvent-based contact cement (laminate work), hot-melt EVA or PUR adhesives (edge banding).

Hazard + pictograms. Solvent contact cement: Flame, Health Hazard, Exclamation Mark. Hot melt: primarily thermal burn; some carry Exclamation Mark.

PPE. Contact cement: nitrile gloves, eye protection, organic-vapour respirator in unventilated areas. Hot melt: heat-resistant gloves near applicator, eye protection.

If exposed. Contact-cement skin contact: soap and water before it cures, never use solvent. Hot-melt burn: cool with running water 10–15 min, do not peel the hardened adhesive off (takes skin with it), medical attention if burn is larger than a quarter.

If spilled. Contact cement: same as solvent finishes (flammable liquid procedure). Hot melt: let cool and solidify, scrape, dispose.

5. PVA / yellow wood glue

What it is. Polyvinyl acetate (Titebond II/III etc.). The everyday assembly glue.

Hazard + pictograms. Low overall, but skin sensitization and eye irritation with daily contact. Exclamation Mark (some products carry none).

PPE. Nitrile gloves, safety glasses, eye-wash within reach.

If exposed. Skin: soap and water. Eye: 15-minute flush, medical attention if irritation persists.

If spilled. Wipe with water before it cures; peel/scrape after.

6. Lacquer thinner and mineral spirits

What it is. Solvent blends used for thinning, cleanup, gun-flushing. Lacquer thinner is the aggressive one (acetone / toluene / MEK blend); mineral spirits is the milder petroleum distillate.

Hazard + pictograms. Flame (very low flash point on lacquer thinner), Exclamation Mark (defatting, irritation), Health Hazard (chronic inhalation). Aspiration hazard if swallowed — chemical pneumonia.

PPE. Nitrile or solvent-rated gloves, safety glasses, organic-vapour respirator for sustained use.

If exposed. Skin: soap and water — never use more solvent to clean off solvent. Eye: 15-minute flush. Inhalation: fresh air, medical if dizziness persists. Ingestion: do not induce vomiting, Poison Control, bring SDS.

If spilled. Same flammable-liquid protocol as item 2.

7. Cleaning solvents (denatured alcohol, acetone, isopropanol)

What it is. Surface-prep and hand-cleanup solvents.

Hazard + pictograms. Flame (acetone is particularly volatile), Exclamation Mark.

PPE. Nitrile gloves, safety glasses, ventilation.

If exposed / spilled. Same flammable-liquid protocol as lacquer thinner.

8. Compressed air and pneumatic systems

What it is. Shop air at 90–120 psi plus the pneumatic tools and spray guns it drives.

Hazard. Physical, not chemical — but serious. Air injected through skin can cause embolism (life-threatening). Eye injury from debris when blowing off a workpiece. Hearing damage from sustained exhaust noise.

PPE. Safety glasses always when using compressed air, hearing protection, gloves.

If exposed. Air-injection injury: call 911 even if the entry wound looks small. Do not wait and see. Eye debris: eye-wash, medical attention if anything is embedded.

9. Forklift propane and forklift batteries

What it is. LPG cylinders for propane forklifts; lead-acid batteries for electric forklifts.

Hazard + pictograms. Propane: Flame, Gas Cylinder (flammable + pressure + asphyxiant). Lead-acid battery: Corrosion (sulfuric acid), Flame (hydrogen gas during charging).

PPE. Propane changeover: safety glasses, gloves — specific forklift-propane certification required first. Battery charging / fluid check: safety glasses, face shield, acid-resistant apron and gloves; do not bypass charging-area ventilation.

If exposed. Propane leak (smell of gas): leave the area, no ignition sources, alert supervisor. Battery-acid skin/eye contact: immediate 15-minute flush, medical attention.

If spilled. Battery acid: neutralize with sodium bicarbonate slurry per SDS, hazardous-waste disposal. Propane leak: evacuate, ventilate, no electrical switches.

Common mistakes + how to recover

"My respirator is on the wrong cartridge — but it's the same brand." Cartridges are colour-coded for hazard class. An organic-vapour cartridge will not stop ammonia; a dust filter will not stop solvent vapour. Check the cartridge against SDS Section 8 every time.

"I used solvent to clean lacquer off my hands." Now you have solvent absorbing into your skin. Soap and water for skin cleanup, not solvent.

"The dust collector is making a weird noise but I have panels to cut." Stop the job. A failing dust collector is a combustible-dust explosion risk. Tell your supervisor.

"I'll only use the contact cement for 30 seconds — I don't need the respirator." A 30-second exposure can trigger a sensitization reaction. Sensitization is not reversible. Wear the respirator every time.

Quiz (5 questions, applied)

1. You're sanding solid walnut for two hours on the random-orbit sander with dust collection running. Do you need a respirator?

Yes — N95 minimum. Walnut dust is a recognized carcinogen and sensitizer. Dust collection reduces but does not eliminate exposure.

2. A coworker spills about 2 L of lacquer thinner on the finishing room floor and reaches for a mop. What do you tell them?

Stop — do not mop (spreads vapour, fire risk). Eliminate ignition sources, do not flip electrical switches. Ventilate. Get the spill kit, absorb with clay/vermiculite (not water). Dispose in the metal waste container. Tell the supervisor and log the incident.

3. You're about to mix acid catalyst into a conversion varnish for the first time. What is your first PPE step and what must be within reach?

Face shield + chemical apron + butyl or neoprene gloves (not standard nitrile — confirm in SDS Section 8) + respirator with cartridge from the SDS. The eye-wash station and emergency shower must be within 10 seconds reach before you open the bottle.

4. A nail gun misfires and you feel a sting on your palm. The puncture is barely visible and there is no nail. What do you do?

Treat as compressed-air injection injury and call 911. Do not wait — air under the skin can cause embolism or serious tissue damage. Notify your supervisor.

5. Hot-melt adhesive drips onto your hand at the edge bander and hardens. What do you do?

Cold running water 10–15 minutes. Do not peel the adhesive off — it takes skin with it. First-aid responder decides whether to leave it until it releases naturally or whether medical attention is needed.

Your Rights, Responsibilities, and Emergency Response

Who this lesson is for

Every Southbrook employee. This is the last lesson of the WHMIS base course and it covers two things you need cold: what you are legally entitled to (and obligated to do) under Canadian occupational health and safety law, and what to do in the first 60 seconds when something goes wrong.

Where this lives on the site

Physical locations matter here. Your trainer will walk you to each of these during the in-person session and mark them on a printed shop-floor map posted in the floor office.

Eye-wash station — TBD, trainer to fill in (typical: finishing room, near solvent decant)

Emergency shower — TBD, trainer to fill in (typical: finishing room or chemical storage)

Fire extinguishers (Class ABC at each station; Class B in finishing room for flammable liquids)

First-aid kit + AED — TBD, trainer to fill in

Spill kits (finishing room, glue area, warehouse)

Muster point — TBD, trainer to fill in (typical: parking lot, away from building)

Joint Health and Safety Committee notice board → Floor Office

Emergency contact list → at every phone + shop entrance

If any of these is blocked, covered, broken, or out of supply, that is a stop-the-job problem. Tell your supervisor immediately.

Recognition + response

Part 1 — Your three rights under Canadian OHS

Guaranteed to every worker by occupational health and safety legislation. Not perks Southbrook grants you — legal rights you cannot sign away.

Right 1 — The right to know. You have the right to know about the hazards in your workplace and how to handle them safely. You are entitled to training on every hazardous product you work with or near, access to the SDS for every product on site, legible labels on every container, and information about new hazards as they are introduced. If your supervisor blocks any of these — that violates your right to know. Escalate.

Right 2 — The right to participate. You can ask questions, raise hazards, suggest improvements. You can participate in the Joint Health and Safety Committee (JHSC) — Ontario law requires one at workplaces with 20+ workers. The JHSC inspects the workplace, investigates incidents, and recommends improvements. You can be a member; the committee notice board lists current members and how to nominate yourself.

Right 3 — The right to refuse unsafe work. You can refuse work you believe is dangerous to yourself or another worker. This is the strongest right and the most misunderstood. The Ontario OHS Act process:

  1. You believe work is unsafe (equipment, environment, or another person's behaviour creates a likely danger).
  2. Report the refusal to your supervisor, verbally is fine.
  3. Stay at a safe place near the workstation while the investigation happens — you are still on the clock; refusal is not walking off the job.
  4. Your supervisor investigates in the presence of a JHSC worker representative (or another worker chosen by you).
  5. Hazard resolved → back to work. Still unsafe → the Ministry of Labour, Immigration, Training and Skills Development is called; an inspector decides.

You cannot be punished for refusing in good faith. Reprisal — firing, demotion, worse hours, worse station — is a separate offence.

Part 2 — Internal Responsibility System (IRS)

The three rights live inside the IRS: everyone in the workplace has a role in safety, scaled to their authority.

  • Workers — follow safe procedures, use PPE, report hazards.
  • Supervisors — enforce procedures, train, respond to reports, fix what they can.
  • Employer (Southbrook) — provide safe workplaces, equipment, procedures, training, PPE.
  • JHSC — keep the system honest by inspecting, investigating, recommending.

The IRS is layered. Everyone contributes. Everyone is accountable.

Part 3 — Emergency response

The first 60 seconds determine the outcome. Memorise these.

Small chemical spill (under ~1 L, non-acutely-toxic): Eliminate ignition sources → ventilate → spill kit + PPE per SDS Sections 6 + 8 → contain with absorbent → scoop into approved waste container → tell supervisor → log the incident.

Large spill, or any spill of acutely toxic / corrosive / unknown product: Evacuate the immediate area (move upwind / to fresh air) → alert the supervisor → sound the building alarm if the spill threatens the area beyond the room → do not attempt cleanup unless trained for that product with the right PPE on → account for everyone at the muster point.

Skin exposure: Remove contaminated clothing (cut it off if it sticks) → flush with water at emergency shower or sink → 15 minutes minimum for corrosives, time specified on the SDS for others → tell supervisor → medical attention per SDS Section 4 → bring the SDS to the medical responder.

Eye exposure: Get to the eye-wash immediately — do not stop to ask permission. Hold eyelids open and flush 15 minutes minimum. Remove contact lenses if present and you can do so without delaying the flush. Get medical attention. Bring the SDS.

Inhalation: Get the person to fresh air. If you cannot enter without your own PPE, do not go in — call for help. Loosen tight clothing. If not breathing: CPR if trained, call 911. Get medical attention; bring the SDS. Some inhalation effects are delayed and need observation.

Ingestion: Do not induce vomiting unless SDS Section 4 specifically says to (most solvents — vomiting is the wrong response; aspiration into the lungs is worse). Call Poison Control (Ontario: 1-800-268-9017) or 911. Bring the SDS.

Fire — wood dust: Different from a normal fire. Heat and air movement can flash dust into an explosion. Sound the alarm → evacuate → call 911. Do not use compressed air or a fan to clear smoke (re-suspends dust). Class ABC extinguisher for small surface fires. For a dust-collector fire: evacuate and wait for the fire department — opening the collector can cause a flash.

Fire — solvent / flammable liquid: Sound the alarm → evacuate → call 911. Class B extinguisher if the fire is smaller than a wastebasket and you have an escape route at your back. Never use water on a solvent fire — spreads burning liquid. Get out if it is bigger than you can handle in 30 seconds.

Chain of report. Every incident — exposure, spill, fire, near miss — goes up this chain: immediate supervisor → safety officer / JHSC → 911 for medical / fire / hazardous-materials release beyond a small spill → Ministry of Labour for serious workplace injuries (the safety officer handles this notification; your job is to make sure the safety officer knows). Filing a report does not get you in trouble. Not filing one does.

Common mistakes + how to recover

"I'd feel like a snitch if I called the JHSC about my supervisor." The JHSC exists for exactly this. Concerns are confidential when you ask. Not raising a hazard because you are uncomfortable is how people get hurt.

"I refused to do a task and I'm worried I'll get fired." Refusing unsafe work in good faith is protected. Firing or punishing you for that is reprisal — a separate offence. Document everything (date, time, what you refused, who you told). Talk to the JHSC.

"I splashed something in my eye but it doesn't hurt much — I'll finish my task first." Get to the eye-wash now. Chemical eye damage is often painless until the damage is done. The 15-minute window is in regulation for a reason.

"There was a small lacquer-thinner spill and I cleaned it up with a mop, then went on with my day." Mopping is wrong (spreads vapour, fire risk). And the incident must be logged even if nobody was hurt — a near miss this week is an injury next week if uncorrected.

"The eye-wash station was being used as a coat rack and I didn't say anything." That is the single most dangerous WHMIS failure on a shop floor. The eye-wash must be unobstructed and tested weekly. Move the coats; tell your supervisor.

Quiz (5 questions, applied)

1. Your supervisor asks you to spray a new conversion varnish in the spray booth. The booth exhaust fan is not working — you can see the booth fogging up within seconds. What are your options under Ontario OHS?

Exercise your right to refuse unsafe work. Tell the supervisor verbally that you refuse because the exhaust is not functioning. Stay nearby — you are still on the clock. The supervisor investigates with a JHSC worker representative. Fixed → you resume. Still unsafe in your judgement → Ministry of Labour is called. You cannot be punished for refusing in good faith.

2. A coworker gets contact cement on the back of their hand and says "it's fine, I'll keep going." What do you tell them?

Wash it off with soap and water before it cures. Solvent-based contact cement is a skin sensitizer; repeated contact builds a chronic reaction. Thirty seconds of washing is cheaper than the medical leave later.

3. You walk past the finishing room and see lacquer thinner spreading across the floor — maybe 4 L. The supervisor is on break. What do you do, in order?

(a) Do not enter the spill area; do not flip electrical switches nearby. (b) Yell to clear the immediate area. (c) Call the supervisor — phone, radio, or send a coworker. (d) Open doors / ventilation upstream. (e) If the spill is growing toward an ignition source, sound the alarm. (f) Stay out until trained responders arrive with the spill kit and respirators. Do not attempt cleanup yourself.

4. You're a JHSC member. The committee notices three incidents in two months involving the same edge-banding adhesive. What can the committee do?

Recommend the employer investigate and correct — change product, change procedure, add PPE, add training. If the employer does not respond, the committee can raise it with the Ministry of Labour. Right to participate is exercised through exactly this mechanism.

5. Someone collapses in the finishing room after spraying for two hours. They are conscious but disoriented and breathing rapidly. You are not sure what they sprayed. What is your first call and what do you bring to the responders?

Call 911 first. Move them to fresh air only if you can do so without exposing yourself (do not enter if the air is still vapour- heavy and you have no respirator). Grab the SDS for the product they were spraying — responders need it for treatment. Tell the supervisor. Account for everyone else who was in the room.

What this lesson does NOT cover

  • Pictograms → lesson 16.2. Labels → 16.3. SDS → 16.4. Shop hazards → 16.5.
  • Hands-on first aid, CPR, AED training — separate certified courses.
  • Spill-team training (full PPE + procedure for major spills) — separate certified training for designated responders.
  • Forklift, spray-booth, and acid-catalyst certifications — separate training with sign-off.

End of course

This is the last lesson in WHMIS Base Training. You have covered:

  • 16.1 — What WHMIS is, three pillars, legal frame, responsibilities.
  • 16.2 — The 9 pictograms.
  • 16.3 — Supplier labels (6 elements) and workplace labels (3 elements).
  • 16.4 — How to read an SDS in 60 seconds.
  • 16.5 — The actual hazardous products at Southbrook.
  • 16.6 — Your three rights, the IRS, and emergency response.

You refresh annually, sooner if a new hazard is introduced. You take job-specific training for any station that requires it — spray booth, forklift, acid-catalyst mixing — separately, with sign-off.

WHMIS is not a one-time stamp on a form. It is how everyone in this shop goes home in the same condition they came in.
